limitations.text: The default modern-v1 plugin is compiled with --release 11 (Java 11 bytecode/API target); the JVM loading it must support that class format. This target does not establish a Java 11 lifecycle point. The opt-in legacy-basic-v1 profile uses a separate Java 6-targeted collector; executed combinations are recorded separately.

legacy-basic-v1 is an explicit x86_64-linux Nix scope with a mandatory live legacyJvmAdapter and actual Ant/Ivy packages. The SDK and manager must have the published output/home/executable/runtime-home identities; version strings never choose replacement SDK inputs. The recorded tested tuple is separate from packaged defaults and bytecode targets.

The legacy profile exposes dependencies and a source/class tree. Its archive is not native artifact publication fidelity. Packaging/publication tasks, task containers, nested Ant, Javadoc/JUnit tasks, project composition and projections are unsupported. Arbitrary custom-task introspection, additional versions, ARM support and version ranges are not established.

projectSelections.description: Select legacy-basic-v1 explicitly and supply the actual Ant package in the Nix scope; this opt-in profile is restricted to x86_64-linux.
projectSelections.name: Apache Ant

projectSelections.description: For legacy-basic-v1, supply the actual Ivy package in the same Nix scope; its native API and origin belong to the recorded tuple.
projectSelections.name: Apache Ivy

projectSelections.description: For legacy-basic-v1, supply a live SDK adapter with explicit manager executable and runtime home. Nix contexts retain the actual SDK inputs.
projectSelections.name: JDK

projectSelections.description: For legacy-basic-v1, compilation must use the SDK home/compiler bound by the live adapter. It is a Nix value rather than a version string or serialized store path.
projectSelections.name: JDK

projectSelections.description: Forked Java tasks in legacy-basic-v1 must use the adapter’s declared manager executable or runtime-home Java executable. The recorded tuple uses the same SDK for every role; independent runtime SDKs have no recorded point.
projectSelections.name: JDK

notes: Released in v0.1.4 with the explicit legacy-basic-v1 Nix scope: Ant 1.5.4, Ivy 2.4.0 and Azul Zulu JDK 6.0.119 (observed java.version 1.6.0-119) on x86_64-linux. The same declared SDK runs the native tool, compiler and asserting Java execution.

The caller supplies a live published JVM SDK adapter and actual Ant/Ivy packages. Output, home, executable and runtime-home Nix contexts are retained; serialized lock paths never select or reconstruct an SDK. Actual native process, runtime home and Ant/Ivy/collector JAR origins are checked.

Independent native controls resolve a nonempty direct/transitive graph, select shared 2.0 and evict transitive shared 1.0 with its middle caller edge. Actual collector relock and relocation preserve all three lock files byte for byte. Original project sources remain unchanged.

After prefetch, the origin is stopped and a fresh native build/test runs in an OS network namespace. Retrieved dependency bytes and compiled Main.class bytes match the independent native control; class-file major is 50. Assertions run through a Java task, not a JUnit task. No whole-JAR/POM or published-byte parity claim.

Immutable-source pure evaluation with import-from-derivation disabled, source/class-tree build and deterministic source/class-tree archive rebuild pass. The release is a source/class-tree archive, not native artifact publication fidelity. Packaging/publication, task containers, nested Ant, Javadoc/JUnit tasks, project composition and projections are outside this profile.

Controls cover same-version foreign manager/compiler/runtime rejection before the relevant role actions, same-bytes foreign JAR origins, direct packaging and Sequential/Parallel rejection before earlier target actions, native Ivy warm/fresh cache behavior, sticky pins, named updates and changed-artifact rejection without lock writes. Arbitrary custom-task introspection is not established.

Ordinary unlocked ant warns and executes the selected native tool with original arguments/environment. Explicit prefetch and partial/malformed locks remain errors. These controls establish no additional toolchain tuple, Ant 1.2/Ivy 2.4 compatibility, ARM support or version range.

values.language_tooling_setup:
`prefetch` leaves `node_modules` with ordinary files, so an editor's
TypeScript server, and `tsc`, read the installed types as after a plain
`bun install`. bun projects bring TypeScript and their `@types` packages
as dependencies, so `bun.lock` holds what the editor reads, and it is
there after `prefetch`.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/bun-purifier'
bun-purifier lock
bun-purifier prefetch
bun run build
bun test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Ruby LSP works offline when the project locks it like any other gem:

```ruby
group :development do
  gem "ruby-lsp", require: false
end
```

Then run `bundler-purifier lock` and `bundler-purifier prefetch`, and start
the editor from the `nix shell` environment. Run the language server
through `bundle exec ruby-lsp`. Ruby LSP uses the project's bundle when the
Gemfile has it, and needs no download of its own.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/bundler-purifier'
bundler-purifier lock
bundler-purifier prefetch
bundle exec rake

values.language_tooling_setup:
`prefetch` puts the `haskell-language-server` of the toolchain and the `cabal`
shim first on `PATH`. An editor started from that shell, or with that
`PATH`, loads the project through the shim, so the build tool calls of the
language server go to the locked sources and nothing is downloaded.
A `.envrc` with the `eval` line from [Working offline](reference.html#working-offline) does
the same for direnv.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/cabal-purifier'
cabal-purifier lock
eval "$(cabal-purifier prefetch)"
cabal build
cabal test

Point the editor at the `rust-analyzer` of the `cargo-purifier` package,
for example `target/cargo-purifier/prefetch/tools/bin/rust-analyzer` after
a prefetch. It runs `cargo metadata` and `cargo check` through the cargo
wrapper, so it loads the workspace and its dependencies from the vendored
sources, and it reads the standard library's sources from the package
set's rust-src.

cargo-purifier lock
cargo-purifier prefetch
cargo build
cargo test

clojure-cli-purifier.summary: Locked, Nix-resolved dependencies for Clojure CLI.

values.language_tooling_setup:
[clojure-lsp](https://clojure-lsp.io) computes the classpath with
`clojure -Spath`, so it reads the locked downloads when the editor's
environment has `.clojure-cli-purifier/bin` first on `PATH`, such as
through direnv. In a project with a `bb.edn`, clojure-lsp asks babashka for
the classpath, and `.lsp/config.edn` points it at `deps.edn`:

```clojure
{:project-specs [{:project-path "deps.edn"
                  :classpath-cmd ["clojure" "-A:test" "-Spath"]}]}
```

clojure-lsp analyzes the jars on the classpath, which hold the Clojure
sources, and needs no other download.
values.quickstart:
nix shell \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#clojure' \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#cli'
clojure-cli-purifier lock \
  --build '-T:build uber' --test '-M:test'
clojure-cli-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/.clojure-cli-purifier/bin:$PATH"
clojure -T:build uber
clojure -M:test

The initial cache sets `CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS`, so the configure
writes `build/compile_commands.json`. clangd and other tools that read it
find every dependency's headers in the prefetched sources, offline. The
development shell of this flake has clangd; a project's own shell takes
`clang-tools` from nixpkgs.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/cmake-purifier#toolchain'
cmake-purifier lock
cmake-purifier prefetch
cmake -B build -C .cmake-purifier/initial-cache.txt
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build

values.language_tooling_setup:
PHP editors and language servers, such as phpactor and Intelephense, read
the project's `vendor` directory. A Composer dist holds the full source of
its package, so `composer install` after a prefetch gives the editor the
full source of every package. The development shell has phpactor.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/composer-purifier#toolchain'
composer-purifier lock
composer-purifier prefetch
composer install
composer test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Point the editor at `.conda-purifier/env/bin/python`, the way you would
point it at a conda environment. In VS Code, run "Python: Select
Interpreter". For pyright, pass
`--pythonpath .conda-purifier/env/bin/python`. Run
`conda-purifier prefetch` first, so that the interpreter exists.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/conda-purifier'
conda-purifier lock
conda-purifier prefetch
conda activate ./.conda-purifier/env
python -m pytest

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor that starts `deno lsp` from the `PATH` of the development shell
gets the wrapper, so the language server reads the locked downloads. An
import the lock covers resolves, and one it does not is reported as an
uncached URL, as Deno reports any module missing from its cache. The
language server needs what `prefetch` realizes.

deno test
deno task

values.language_tooling_setup:
After a prefetch, the packages are in your NuGet package folder and every
project is restored, so a language server that reads a project through
MSBuild (the Roslyn language server, csharp-ls or OmniSharp) works with no
network. Run it with the locked SDK, which `prefetch` links at
`.dotnet-purifier/sdk` next to the lockfile: put `.dotnet-purifier/sdk/bin`
first on its `PATH` and set `DOTNET_ROOT` to
`.dotnet-purifier/sdk/share/dotnet`. Navigation into
a package's code decompiles it locally; source files that SourceLink
downloads need the network.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/dotnet-purifier'
dotnet-purifier lock
dotnet-purifier dotnet build
dotnet-purifier dotnet test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Run `serve-d` from the same shell as DUB. Its wrapper activates the locked
source paths and completion tools. A project session in `.dub-purifier/sessions/` holds writable
application caches and GC roots for its immutable dependencies and SDK.

```sh
dub-purifier shell
serve-d
```

Ignore `.dub/`, `.dub-purifier/` and generated application binaries in Git.
There is no generated Nix devshell.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/dub-purifier'
dub-purifier lock
dub-purifier prefetch
dub run
dub test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers find `elm`, `elm-test` and `elm-format` on
`PATH`, and the packages through `ELM_HOME`. The tools in
`elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` set `ELM_HOME` themselves, so putting that
directory first on `PATH` is all an editor needs. The same directory holds
`elm-language-server`, which runs the language server with that `PATH`:

```zsh
PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH" code .
```

With direnv, the line `PATH_add elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` in `.envrc`
does the same. The language server sometimes hangs while it starts, and
restarting it from the editor fixes that.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/elm-purifier'
elm-purifier lock
elm-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH"
elm make src/Main.elm
elm-test

values.language_tooling_setup:
The development shell has gopls. gopls runs the `go` on its `PATH`, so an
editor that starts gopls from the shell resolves from the same locked
downloads, offline after a prefetch. An editor that starts gopls itself
needs the shell's `PATH`, such as through direnv with `use flake`.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/go-purifier'
go-purifier lock
go build ./...
go test ./...

Prefetch does not rewrite project/global properties. This mechanism establishes no Java6/7 or version-range compatibility claim.

values.language_tooling_setup:
An IDE imports a Gradle build with its own Gradle run, through the Gradle
tooling API: IntelliJ IDEA, and Eclipse and VS Code through Buildship and
jdtls. The init script that `prefetch` installs applies to those runs too,
so the import reads the locked downloads. The lock run resolves the
sources and the javadoc of every library, so an IDE that attaches them
finds them in the lock. An IDE set to use the Gradle wrapper finds the
distribution that `prefetch` linked. One set to a local distribution can
use `.gradle-purifier/distribution` beside the lockfile.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/gradle-purifier'

gradle-purifier prefetch

```sh
jsonnet-language-server -J vendor --eval-diags
```

values.language_tooling_setup:
`julia-purifier language-server` runs [LanguageServer.jl](https://github.com/julia-vscode/LanguageServer.jl)
on standard input and output for the project, from the environment that
`prefetch` realized. Point the Julia language-server setting of the editor at
this command, in the directory of the project. The server finds the
dependencies in the prefetched depot and needs no network; its index goes
under `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/julia-purifier`.

values.language_tooling_setup:
After `prefetch`, `lua_modules` holds every dependency as a standard
LuaRocks tree. Point the language server at it. For
[lua-language-server](https://luals.github.io), a `.luarc.json` in the
project root sets its library path:

```json
{
  "runtime.version": "Lua 5.4",
  "workspace.library": ["lua_modules/share/lua/5.4"]
}
```

For LuaJIT and Lua 5.1, the directory is `lua_modules/share/lua/5.1`.

`prefetch` realizes the rocks, and the language server comes from your own
editor setup, such as the nixpkgs package `lua-language-server`.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/luarocks-purifier'
luarocks-purifier lock
luarocks-purifier prefetch
luarocks-purifier luarocks make
luarocks-purifier luarocks test

limitations.text: Maven 2 and 3.0 capture defaults to Java 8; a selected JAVA_HOME can choose a different JVM, which project plugins must support.
Maven before 3.3.1 does not read .mvn/maven.config. Use the prefetched .maven-purifier/bin/mvn launcher for locked development with those versions.

Native incoming dependency selection requires Maven 3 or newer; Maven 2.2.1 can consume Nix inputs through the sandbox builder. The legacy Maven 2/3.0 recording path cannot use authenticated repositories that require Maven-specific transports.
The Maven 3 recording classes target Java 8 bytecode; Maven 4-specific recording classes target Java 17. The selected JVM must also meet Maven and project-plugin requirements.

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor that imports a Maven build, such as VS Code or Neovim through
jdtls, or IntelliJ IDEA, runs a Maven of its own. After a prefetch, make
`.maven-purifier/settings.xml` the editor's Maven user settings,
`java.configuration.maven.userSettings` for jdtls or *User settings file*
in IntelliJ IDEA, and the editor resolves from the locked files without the
network: dependencies, their source jars, and the plugins of its own Maven.

The lock holds the default plugins of the Maven that jdtls embeds, which
the lock run reads from the jdtls of maven-purifier's nixpkgs. An editor whose Maven has other
default plugin versions finds them missing offline, unless the build pins
the version of every plugin it uses in `<pluginManagement>`, as we
recommend; then every Maven asks for the locked versions.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/maven-purifier'
maven-purifier lock
maven-purifier prefetch
mvn test
mvn package

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors such as Metals (in VS Code) and IntelliJ IDEA talk to Mill through
the Build Server Protocol (BSP), and start Mill with the command in
`.bsp/mill-bsp.json`. Write that file through the purifier:

```zsh
mill-purifier mill mill.bsp.BSP/install
```

The command it names is a script under `~/.cache/mill-purifier` that runs
`mill-purifier mill` in the build, so the editor's Mill also runs offline
from the lockfile. The lock run starts Mill's BSP server and asks it what
an editor asks first (the build targets and the sources of their
dependencies), so the server's own libraries and the source jars an editor
shows are in the lock. The script names the mill-purifier package it was
written by; run the install again after updating mill-purifier.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/mill-purifier'
mill-purifier lock
mill-purifier mill core.compile
mill-purifier mill core.test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Point the editor's Elixir language server at
`_build/mix-purifier/toolchain/bin/elixir-ls`, which is nixpkgs' ElixirLS
with Hex on its code path. ElixirLS fetches its own files when it first
starts, so `mix-purifier prefetch` starts it once, with the network, to
fetch them. Afterwards it starts with no network.
`mix-purifier prefetch --no-editor` skips that step.
values.quickstart:
nix shell \
  'github:nix-purifiers/mix-purifier' \
  'github:nix-purifiers/mix-purifier#toolchain'
mix-purifier lock
mix-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/_build/mix-purifier/toolchain/bin:$PATH"
mix compile
mix test

```sh
nim check src/example.nim
```

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers read `node_modules`, which `npm ci` through
the wrapper fills as plain npm does, so they need no setup of their own.
An editor that runs npm itself (task runners, script panels) gets the
wrapper when it starts from `nix shell` with the toolchain package,
or from your usual environment configuration with the wrapper on `PATH`.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/npm-purifier#toolchain'
npm-purifier lock
npm ci
npm run build
npm test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Lock the language server and the formatter as tools:

```zsh
opam-purifier lock --tool ocaml-lsp-server --tool ocamlformat
opam-purifier prefetch
```

opam solves the tools together with the project, so they agree on shared
versions, and the Nix build leaves them out. `prefetch` installs them into
`_opam`, and `source .opam-purifier/env.sh` puts `ocamllsp` and
`ocamlformat` on `PATH`. Start the editor from that environment, or from
direnv. The server runs offline.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/opam-purifier'
opam-purifier lock
opam-purifier prefetch
source .opam-purifier/env.sh
dune build
dune test

```elisp
(require 'package)

(setq package-selected-packages '(vertico))
```

Open a shell containing the CLI and Emacs wrapper:

tree; package byte compilation runs in the Nix sandbox.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/package-el-purifier'
package-el-purifier lock
package-el-purifier prefetch

values.language_tooling_setup:
`prefetch` installs the project into `.venv`, with the development groups.
Point the editor's Python interpreter at `.venv/bin/python`, and its
language server finds every dependency there with no network. Install the
language server itself from Nix.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/pdm-purifier'
pdm-purifier lock
pdm-purifier prefetch
eval "$(pdm venv activate)"
pytest

values.language_tooling_setup:
Point the editor at `.venv`, as for any virtual environment. For pyright
and basedpyright, `prefetch` makes `.venv` in the project root, where they
look for it by default. The packages in `.venv` hold their sources, so
go-to-definition and type information work offline. The language server
itself comes from your editor setup, such as nixpkgs' `pyright`.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/pip-purifier'
pip-purifier lock
pip-purifier prefetch
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pytest

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor for Python needs the interpreter of the `.venv`, with the
project's packages in it. Point the editor's Python at `.venv/bin/python`,
or let it find `.venv` in the project, as Pyright and the Python extension
of VS Code do. A Python editor reads the project's packages from the
`.venv`, which `prefetch` installs, and asks for no downloads of its own,
so `prefetch` fetches nothing for the editor beyond the `.venv`. The
language server comes from the editor's installation.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/pipenv-purifier'
pipenv-purifier lock
pipenv-purifier prefetch
. .venv/bin/activate
pytest

values.language_tooling_setup:
For a Python environment, select `.pixi/envs/default/bin/python` as the
editor's interpreter. For another environment, substitute its name.
Prefetch supplies `pyright` and `pyright-langserver` in the wrapper package;
start the editor from the same `nix shell` so those workers are available.
Language servers declared as environment dependencies are available through
`pixi shell` as well.

The editor check starts a real language server and verifies that its
definition lookup reaches the locked `idna` package in the environment.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/pixi-purifier'
pixi-purifier lock
pixi-purifier prefetch
pixi run check

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor's language server, such as the TypeScript server, reads
`node_modules`. An offline install writes the same `node_modules` an online
one does, so the editor works as it does with pnpm alone, with the network
cut off after a prefetch.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/pnpm-purifier'
alias pnpm=pnpm-purifier
pnpm-purifier lock
pnpm install
pnpm run build
pnpm test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers, such as pyright, read the project's virtual
environment, which the offline install fills like any other `poetry
install`. They download nothing.

setuptools installs an editable path dependency through an import hook by
default, which pyright and other type checkers do not follow. This happens
with or without the purifier. Poetry can ask setuptools for its compat mode
instead, which writes a plain path entry, in the project's `poetry.toml`:

```toml
[installer.build-config-settings.<package>]
editable_mode = "compat"
```
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/poetry-purifier'
poetry purifier lock
poetry purifier prefetch
poetry install
eval "$(poetry env activate)"
pytest

values.language_tooling_setup:
The toolchain has `elp`, the
[Erlang Language Platform](https://whatsapp.github.io/erlang-language-platform/),
which loads the project by running rebar3. Run your editor inside
`nix shell`, or put the toolchain on its `PATH`, and `elp` finds the
rebar3 of the toolchain, which reads the locked downloads. After a
prefetch the editor needs no network.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/rebar3-purifier'
rebar3-purifier lock
rebar3 compile
rebar3 eunit

values.language_tooling_setup:
R's language server is the R package languageserver, which editors such as
VS Code, Emacs and Neovim start for completion and diagnostics. Add it to the
project with renv like any other package. `prefetch` then installs it with
the rest of the library: point the editor's R at
`.renv-purifier/prefetch/R/bin/R`, or start it from `packages.env`. RStudio
and Emacs Speaks Statistics run an ordinary R session, which works the same
way.

values.language_tooling_setup:
An editor imports the build through sbt's build server, and asks it for
the sources of every dependency (`buildTarget/dependencySources`, which
runs `updateClassifiers`). The lock run resolves what a
`dependencySources` request needs: it runs `updateClassifiers` for every
project at its default Scala version, unpublished projects included, and
`updateSbtClassifiers` for the sources of sbt and of the build's plugins.
An editor that imports the build then resolves those sources from the
lock, with the network cut off.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/sbt-purifier#sbt'
sbt nixLock
sbt compile
sbt test

scala-cli-purifier.summary: Locked, Nix-resolved dependencies for Scala CLI.

values.language_tooling_setup:
```zsh
scala-cli setup-ide .
```

run through the wrapper, configures Metals, or any other editor that speaks
the Build Server Protocol, to build the project offline on the prefetched
downloads: it points the launch command in `.bsp/scala-cli.json` at the
wrapper, which starts scala-cli's build server with the locked cache and
the offline mirror. Run it again after `lock`.

The lock run opens the project the way an editor does, and compiles it on
the Bloop compilation server that serves an editor, so the lockfile holds
what an editor asks for, such as the source jars of the dependencies and
the compiler bridge of Bloop. `lock --no-ide` locks without them, for a
smaller lockfile.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/scala-cli-purifier'
scala-cli-purifier lock --test
scala-cli-purifier prefetch
scala-cli run .
scala-cli test .

values.language_tooling_setup:
The toolchain includes sourcekit-lsp, and `prefetch` also writes the
workspace state into `.build/index-build`, where sourcekit-lsp builds its
background index. Editor support does not work yet: the sourcekit-lsp 6.3.3
in nixpkgs cannot find the SourceKit plugin of its toolchain and cannot
create a build server, so it resolves no symbols, with or without
swiftpm-purifier.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/swiftpm-purifier#toolchain'
swiftpm-purifier lock
swift build
swift test

values.language_tooling_setup:
```sh
typst watch main.typ
typst eval --in main.typ 'query(heading).len()'
tinymist lsp
```

Tinymist uses the same Nix package paths for diagnostics and source navigation.
Its locked registry prevents package downloads and index refreshes. For an
editor launched from outside the Nix shell:

```sh
typst-purifier exec -- your-editor .
```

The editor must invoke the supplied `tinymist` wrapper. Compiler rendering uses
the pinned embedded fonts. Custom external fonts and editor font overrides are
outside the current scope.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/typst-purifier'
typst-purifier lock
typst compile main.typ

values.language_tooling_setup:
Use the supplied `clangd` with the compile commands generated by CMake:

```sh
clangd --compile-commands-dir=build
```

The CMake wrapper supplies the locked dependency paths and SDK. Existing
arguments selecting vcpkg's standard CMake toolchain or the recorded triplet
are accepted. A different toolchain, feature set, or installed prefix needs
explicit integration rather than silently changing the dependency graph.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/vcpkg-purifier'
vcpkg-purifier lock
vcpkg-purifier prefetch
cmake -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

values.language_tooling_setup:
Generate the normal compilation database, then start clangd from the same shell:

```sh
xmake project -k compile_commands
clangd
```

The compilation database contains the Nix library include paths. The integration
retains the environment and SDK with GC roots in the project session.
A project shell is also available with `xmake-purifier shell`.

Ignore `.xmake/`, `.xmake-purifier/`, `build/` and `compile_commands.json` in Git.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/xmake-purifier'
xmake-purifier lock
xmake-purifier prefetch
xmake
xmake test

values.language_tooling_setup:
JavaScript editors take their tools from the dependencies that Yarn
installs in the project: TypeScript's language server comes from the
`typescript` package, and ESLint and Prettier come from their own
packages. After `yarn-berry-purifier prefetch` and `yarn install`, those
tools are in place and work offline. A project that uses Plug'n'Play needs
Yarn's editor SDK, which `yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks` installs; `@yarnpkg/sdks`
then has to be a dev dependency, so that the purifier lockfile records it.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/yarn-berry-purifier#toolchain'
yarn-berry-purifier lock
yarn install
yarn run build
yarn test

native.text: Prerequisites: {facts.runtime_requirements}.
Commit the lockfiles: {facts.lockfiles}.
Locking excludes `{facts.generated_cache_directory}` from the native build context. Also commit the updated ignore file.
The native lock records exact revisions; its companion records artifact hashes, original metadata, and resolution configuration.
OCI manifest, configuration, and layer identities retain their native SHA-256 digests. The lock adds platform selections and input fingerprints.

fresh.text:
Run `{commands.lock}` after changing dependency declarations. Relocking resolves dependencies again; it does not retain existing pins.

Run `{commands.prefetch}` before building.
Update one selected dependency with `{commands.named-update} {facts.named_update_example}`. Other selected pins are retained.

locked.text:
Run `{commands.lock}` after changing dependency declarations. Relocking retains existing pins.

Run `{commands.update}` to update dependencies, then `{commands.prefetch}`.
Update one selected dependency with `{commands.named-update} {facts.named_update_example}`. Other selected pins are retained.

native.text: Keep using the native build and test commands in your working tree. After changing dependency declarations, refresh the lock through the native lock workflow shown above.
Relocking retains existing pins.
Use the development environment for builds, tests, and language tooling so they share the selected dependencies.
The environment supplies a tool wrapper that activates the locked dependencies.
Without an applicable purifier lock, the supplied wrapper warns and runs the tool with its usual dependency resolution.
The native tool reads the prepared project dependencies directly; wrapper activation is not required.

wrapper.text: The development environment supplies a wrapper that runs the build tool with the locked dependencies. Without an applicable purifier lock, it warns and lets the tool use its usual dependency resolution. A stale or invalid lock fails with a repair command.
The supplied wrapper is required for native builds.
The wrapper handles {facts.supported_native_commands}; other commands run normally.

Alternatively, activate the native plugin in the build. Resolve `{facts.native_plugin_coordinate}` from the [native plugin repository]({facts.native_plugin_repository}). Keep bootstrap dependencies separate from application dependencies.
Native Maven bootstrap resolution is impure; use the wrapper for pure plugin resolution.

native.text: Prepare dependencies using the Quickstart workflow before disconnecting. The lock covers the recorded dependency downloads; downloads performed outside that lock need separate inputs.

scoped.text:
Run `{commands.prefetch}` to prepare the locked dependencies. This does not guarantee that the entire build can run offline.

Outside this lock: {facts.offline_limits}.
Prefetch retains {facts.prefetch_components} through garbage-collector roots beside the selected lockfile.

command.text: Configure the Language Server Protocol (LSP) client to launch `{commands.editor}` from the development shell. This puts its language tooling in the same environment as the native build.
Diagnostics and definition lookup work offline after prefetch.
The language server can retrieve source code for locked dependencies.
The launcher prepares Eclipse project metadata with immutable dependency and source JAR paths.

native.text: Integration mechanism: {facts.editor_protocol}.
{values.language_tooling_setup}

builder.text:
Apply `overlays.default` and call `{facts.nix_builder}`.

The result exposes: {facts.build_outputs}.
The project builds in the Nix sandbox.
The builder runs {facts.build_engine} inside a networkless software VM.

native.text: Native development does not require a project Nix build definition. To build in the Nix sandbox, apply `overlays.default` and call `{facts.nix_builder}`.
The builder exposes: {facts.build_outputs}.

preparation.text: Call `{facts.nix_builder}` through `overlays.default` to prepare sources with their native dependency environment. Deployment remains a native tool operation.
